Mechanism of convection-dependence of leveller and its efect on copper pillar
bump filling uniformity
Lei Feng <sup>a</sup>, Cheng-Bin Dong<sup>a</sup>, Ye Huang<sup>a</sup>, Tao Zhang<sup>a</sup> and Jian-Jun Sun <sup>a,b</sup>
<sup>a</sup>College of Chemistry, Fuzhou University, Fuzhou, People’s Republic of China; <sup>b</sup>National Engineering Research Centre of Chemicals for Electronics
Manufacturing (Reconstruction), Xiamen University, Xiamen, People’s Republic of China
ABSTRACT
Metallisation processes, represented by copper pillar bumps (CPBs), are taking the spotlight in the
field of semiconductor advanced packaging. Eficient filling of a uniform, levelling copper layer
within a defined pattern by electroplating is the final goal pursued. In addition to its levelling
capabilities, the leveller Janus Green B (JGB) has an undesired convection-dependence for CPBs,
resulting in a convex front upstream or downstream of the copper filling layer. In this paper, the
JGB is identified as the source of convection-dependence based on an in-situ observation
platform. Electrochemical and spectroscopic evidence supports the conclusion that the reduction
reaction (including protonation of the phenazine ring, hydrogenation reduction or even further
cleavage of the azo group) of JGB also occurs along with the copper electrodeposition process.
The introduction of convection produces a stronger suppression efect and thus a non-uniform
distribution of the filled layer within the microcavity.

Green B
1. Introduction
The deposit leveller takes an important role in plating-related
processes such as copper damascene interconnection,<sup>1–3</sup>
copper pillar bumps,<sup>4,5</sup> and microvias.<sup>6,7</sup> Janus Green B
(JGB) is the commonly used leveller which has been studied
extensively. Kelly et
and Cao et
firstly proposed a
four-component additive containing JGB to achieve the level-
ling efect and suggested a competitive adsorption relation-
ship between these additives. Dow et al.<sup>9–11</sup> found that the
inhibiting efect of JGB was enhanced in the presence of con-
vection and proposed the convection-dependent adsorption
(CDA) theory, suggesting that the CDA behaviour of the addi-
tive was a crucial factor to achieve bottom-up filling. Li et
determined the structure of the reduction product of JGB by
mass spectrometry (MS) and nuclear magnetic resonance
(NMR), and proposed that the reduction product of JGB is
the true leveller in the copper filling process. Mao et al.<sup>13</sup> pro-
vided molecular spectroscopic evidence on the reductive
decomposition of the JGB azo group by in-situ attenuated
total reflection-surface enhanced infrared spectroscopy. Hai
et al.<sup>14</sup> further stated that the consumption of JGB should
also include the reduction of heterocycles. In the present
authors’ previous work, JGB-induced convection-dependence
has been observed,<sup>15</sup> but molecular-level understanding of
its genesis is still absent.
In this study, the JGB-induced convection-dependent
filling process is visualised as benefitting from the CPBs
in-situ observation platform. Cyclic voltammetry (CV), ultra
violet-visible spectroscopy (UV-vis), and in-situ electrochemi
cal surface enhanced Raman spectroscopy (EC-SERS) were
performed to identify the decomposition of JGB. The weaken-
ing of the inhibitory capacity of JGB reduction product rela-
tive to JGB was confirmed by cyclic voltammetry stripping
(CVS). Electrochemical and spectroscopic evidence supports
the idea that inhomogeneous flow field inside the microvia
leads to enhanced renewal of JGB and its reduction product
on the higher flow rate side, and suppressed the deposition
of copper on that side.

3. Results and discussion
3.1. Convection-dependent filling layer profiles due to
leveller JGB
As shown in Figure 1, three diferent convex fronts were cap-
tured during the filling of the MCEs. The combination of PEG
with SPS produced a central convexity, which was caused by
localised adsorption and accumulation of reactant. The intro-
duction of JGB was originally intended to flatten the surface,
but created a downstream bulge problem. Furthermore, an
unexpected contrast is the upstream bias front when only
JGB is added.
Figure 2 shows the surface morphology of MCEs obtained
under diferent additive combinations. While the addition of
PEG and SPS results in refined grains with respect to the
basic plating bath, the lower roughness surface clearly
requires the injection of JGB. Therefore, taking into account
the roles played by the flow field and the leveller JGB in the
convection-dependent morphology generation, it is necess-
ary to reconsider the properties of JGB.
3.2. Electrochemical behaviour of JGB
To understand how JGB produces convection-dependent
efect during deposition, the authors first studied the electro-
chemical behaviour of JGB as shown in Figure 3. The Glass
carbon was chosen as the work electrode due to its wider
anti-interference potentials window and easier identification
of peaks associated with JGB.
Figure 3(a) shows five diferent observed peaks when CV
scans were performed with diferent concentrations of JGB
in an electrolyte consisting of 0.5 M
and 60 ppm Cl<sup>−</sup>.
Peaks 1, 2, 3 and 5 exhibit concentration dependence with
JGB and nearly approach saturation at concentrations
above 800 ppb.
Figure 3(b) illustrates the unexpected electrochemical
behaviour of JGB found during the multi-cycle CV scans.

The efect of scan rate on the peak current was further

It can be inferred from the above experiments that JGB
undergoes the first electron transfer at −0.32 V, followed by
another reduction at −0.46 V. The reduced species will form
a hydrophobic 3D cluster precipitation product on the
surface similar to that observed by Hai et al.,<sup>14</sup> which may
arise from cationic polymerisation reactions during electro-
chemical processes.<sup>17</sup> The reduced species do not leave the
electrode surface directly, while the introduction of convec-
tion can accelerate the exchange between JGB and its
redox, thus exposing new sites for adsorption.
Taking into account that the deposition of copper has
more negative reduction potential than the reduction of
JGB, it is suggested that the reduction of JGB during the
plating process generates a new product (JGB_Red), which
plays a real role in surface inhibition.<sup>12,14,18</sup> The flow rate
diference within the microvias leads to an accelerated
exchange rate of JGB-JGB_Red on the surface, thus exhibiting
diferent deposition rates on the left and right sides of
microvias.
3.3. Spectroscopic study of JGB
To further confirm the consumption of JGB, an electrolysis
experiment was performed with an H-type electrolytic cell
separated by a proton membrane. The solutions containing
the reduced and oxidised products of JGB were obtained
respectively as shown in Figure 4(a). The solution of the
cathode chamber changed from blue to violet colour, while
the blue colour of the anode chamber gradually faded.
Figure 4(b) shows the UV-vis spectra of JGB and its redox
products in neutral and acidic solutions. The aqueous sol-
ution of JGB exhibits absorption peaks at 284, 393, and
603 nm. As a comparison, the maximum absorption peak at
603 nm is significantly broadened in the acidic solution, and
two new peaks at 557 and 616 nm appear. Considering that
the absorbance at 450–750 nm corresponds to the
\scriptstyle { n \to \pi ^ { * } }
transitions (involving electron transitions from lone pairs of
the nitrogen atoms), this diference is supposed to be the
new transitions and the coupling with other transitions due
to the JGB protonation in acidic aqueous solution.
Figure 4(b) also implies the generation of species distinct
from JGB after electrolysis, especially the presence of
maximum absorption peaks at 377 and 557 nm for the
reduction product of JGB (red line). The authors speculate
that this is a further hydrogenation reduction of the azo
group (disappearance of the absorption band at 405 nm cor-
related with the azo group).<sup>19</sup> In contrast, a clear decrease in
the concentration of JGB appears in the anodic compartment
(weakened absorbance).
For comparison, the UV-vis spectra of MEV, which is struc-
turally similar to the phenazine ring of JGB, were also col-
lected in Figure 4(b). The characteristic absorption peaks of
MEV at 377 and 557 nm correspond exactly to the JGB
reduction product. This result confirms that the electrochemi-
cal reduction of JGB will lead to the cleavage of the azo
group. A new peak at 377 nm was also observed for MEV in
acidic solution, corresponding to the protonation of
phenazine.
Subsequently, the decomposition process of JGB was
further investigated by EC-SERS experiments. Based on the

3.4. Mechanism of convection-dependence of leveller
As a final component of this study, the diference in inhibition
of copper deposition by JGB and JGB_Red needs to be eval-
uated. The cyclic voltammetry stripping (CVS) method<sup>27</sup> was
used to compare the changes in the inhibition ability of the
plating solution when JGB or JGB_Red was added to the
basic plating bath (Figure 6).
Figure 6(a) illustrates typical CVS results used to evaluate
additive inhibition capability. Additives with inhibition
ability will slow down the deposition rate of Cu, which
further leads to a decrease in the area of the Cu dissolution
peak at around 0 V.
Figure 6(b) presents the trend of JGB and JGBRP inhibition
factors with potential. The negative reverse potential was
varied from −0.1 to −0.4 V to cover the potential window
for JGB reduction as well as copper deposition. As shown in
Figure 6(b), both JGB and JGBRP exhibited the ability to
inhibit copper deposition. However, when the potential is
shifted negatively to −0.3 V, the inhibition ability of both
decreases significantly, which is attributed to the desorption
of the leveller at more negative potentials.
JGB exhibits a consistently stronger inhibition ability than
its reduction product, indicating that the inhibition ability of
JGB can be maintained at a high level even if it decomposes
when the raw material is suficiently supplied. Therefore, even
with the generation of JGB_Red in actual plating, the wea-
kened inhibition ability of JGB can be compensated for as
long as suficient convection is ensured.
So far, based on the above spectroscopic evidence and
electrochemical studies, the convective dependence exhib-
ited by JGB can be explained: JGB initially protonates in
acidic solutions and subsequently becomes further decom
posed during copper deposition, and the inhibition of the
redox is much weaker. For regions with strong convection
(e.g. mouth of the microvia,<sup>9,10</sup> and downstream of microcav-
ity<sup>15,28</sup>), where suficient raw material supply can maintain the
inhibition ability, the growth of copper can be slowed down,
while, for the weaker convective regions (e.g. bottom of the
microvia, and upstream of microcavity), the inhibition is rela
tively weak, which will be preferred for copper growth.
4. Conclusion
In this paper, the mechanism of convection-dependent mor-
phology induced by the leveller JGB has been investigated
based on an in-situ observation platform simulating the
work conditions of CPBs electrodeposition. The results of
CV. UV-vis. and FC-SERS experiments indicate that the
decomposition of JGB involves the protonation of the phena-
zine ring and the reduction of the azo group. The CVS studies
further indicate that the reduction of JGB will result in a weak
ening of its inhibitory capacity. Enhanced convection can
ensure suficient supply of JGB to maintain its inhibitory
capacity, while the decomposition of JGB in the weak convec-
tion region will deteriorate the capacity. This is believed to be
the reason why the plating layer height distribution is
afected by convection during the filling process. The revel-
ation of this decomposition mechanism will contribute to
the understanding of the role played by phenazine-type
leveller, and facilitate the molecular design of leveller and
the quality control of plating bath in the CPBs and microvia
filling process.
